subject: combined-science

items.q: A sheet of window glass lets almost all of the visible light reaching it pass through, but it absorbs most of the ultraviolet. What does this show?
items.correct: Whether a substance absorbs or transmits a wave can depend on the wavelength of that wave.
items.misconception: A material that looks clear to the eye must be transmitting every wave reaching it.
items.why: Students meet 'transparent' as an everyday word describing what the eye can see through, so they generalise a statement about one narrow band of wavelengths into a statement about the whole spectrum. Nothing they can see contradicts it. Transparency is always transparency to a particular range of wavelengths. Different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength, so glass can be clear to visible light and still absorb ultraviolet.
items.random_wrong: Ultraviolet is absorbed by every substance it meets, whatever that substance is.

items.q: Which statement about how substances behave towards electromagnetic waves is correct?
items.correct: One substance can reflect one wavelength but absorb a different one.
items.misconception: A substance that fails to transmit a wave must have absorbed the whole of it.
items.why: Absorption and transmission are usually introduced as a pair, while reflection is taught in a separate lesson about mirrors, so students do not hold all three possibilities in mind at once. A wave meeting a substance can be transmitted, absorbed or reflected, and in general all three happen in some proportion. You can see a wall at all precisely because it reflects a good deal of the light falling on it.
items.random_wrong: A wave behaves in just the same way in every substance it meets.

items.q: Radio waves from a distant transmitter pass easily through the brick walls of a house, but visible light from outside does not. Which explanation is best?
items.correct: The brick transmits radio waves but reflects and absorbs the light.
items.misconception: Radio waves carry far more energy than light, so they force a way through brick.
items.why: The spectrum is usually taught as a table of waves with a list of uses attached to each, which invites students to treat behaviour as a property of the wave alone rather than of the wave and substance together. Absorption, transmission, reflection and refraction are all interactions between a wave and a substance. The same wavelength behaves differently in different substances, and the same substance behaves differently towards different wavelengths.
items.random_wrong: Brick is not transparent, so no electromagnetic wave at all can cross it.

items.q: A water wave crosses from deep water into shallow water at an angle to the boundary and changes direction. What causes the change of direction?
items.correct: The wave has a different velocity in the shallower water.
items.misconception: The wave bounces off the edge of the shallow part and is pushed aside.
items.why: Refraction is met as a bending of light long before the wave picture is available, so students remember the shape of the ray diagram and invent a mechanical cause for it. A ray diagram on its own shows no change of speed anywhere. The cause is the change of velocity. A wave that travelled at the same velocity in both substances would carry straight on across the boundary, however steeply it met it, and there would be no refraction at all.
items.random_wrong: The shallow water blocks part of the wave, so the rest swings round.

items.q: Light travelling through air enters a glass block, where it travels more slowly. Its frequency does not change. What happens to its wavelength?
items.correct: It gets shorter, because the velocity falls while the frequency stays the same.
items.misconception: It stays the same, because the wavelength is fixed by the lamp producing it.
items.why: Students apply the wave equation without deciding which quantity is fixed by the source and which is fixed by the medium, so whichever of frequency or wavelength they thought of first is held constant. Waves cannot pile up or vanish at a boundary, so the same number arrives each second on both sides and the frequency is unchanged. With the velocity smaller and the frequency fixed, the wavelength must fall.
items.random_wrong: It gets longer, because a slower wave needs more time for each cycle.

items.q: A student is drawing a ray diagram for light passing from air into a glass block. Where should the angle of incidence be measured?
items.correct: Between the incoming ray and the normal drawn at the point it enters.
items.misconception: Between the incoming ray and the flat surface of the glass block itself.
items.why: The boundary is a real drawn line and the normal is an added construction line, so students measure from what is already there. The two angles add to 90°, so the error is systematic rather than random. Every angle in refraction and reflection work is measured from the normal. Always draw the dashed normal first, at the exact point where the ray meets the boundary, and measure both angles from it.
items.random_wrong: Between the incoming ray and the refracted ray inside the block.

items.q: A ray of light travels from air into a glass block along the normal, so the angle of incidence is 0°. What should the ray diagram show?
items.correct: The ray carries straight on through the block without changing course.
items.misconception: The ray bends towards the normal as it enters, then bends back as it leaves.
items.why: Every worked example students see uses a slanted ray, so 'entering glass' and 'bending' become welded together. The 0° case is then treated as an exception to be remembered rather than as a consequence of the geometry. Refraction only turns a wave when one part of the wave front reaches the new substance before the rest. Along the normal the whole front arrives at once, so the wave slows as a whole and travels straight on.
items.random_wrong: The ray bends away from the normal as soon as it crosses into the glass.

items.q: In a wave front diagram, what does each drawn line represent?
items.correct: A line joining points of the wave that are all in phase.
items.misconception: A line drawn parallel to the direction the wave is travelling.
items.why: Students have spent far longer drawing rays than wave fronts, and a ray points along the direction of travel, so the new kind of line is assumed to point the same way. Rays and wave fronts are perpendicular to each other. Draw the fronts as a set of parallel lines, like the crests of a water wave, then draw the ray crossing them at 90°.
items.random_wrong: A line whose spacing is the same in every medium it enters.

items.q: A wave front diagram shows plane wave fronts meeting a boundary at an angle. The wave travels more slowly in the second medium. Why do the fronts change direction?
items.correct: One end of each front enters the slower medium first and is held back, so it pivots.
items.misconception: The whole of each front slows down at the very same instant it crosses.
items.why: Students correctly learn that refraction is caused by a change of speed and stop there, without asking why a change of speed should produce a change of direction rather than simply a slower wave. A change of speed alone does not turn a wave — a wave meeting the boundary head-on slows without deviating. Turning needs the two ends of the front to be moving at different speeds for a moment, which only happens when the front meets the boundary at an angle.
items.random_wrong: The fronts turn because the ray drawn through them is refracted there.

items.q: In Required practical activity 10 a Leslie cube is filled with hot water. An infrared detector is placed the same distance from each vertical face in turn. Which face gives the highest reading?
items.correct: The matt black face, because matt black is the best emitter of infrared.
items.misconception: All four read the same, because the water behind each face is at one temperature.
items.why: Students reach for temperature as the cause of anything to do with heating, and the inside of the cube is not visible, so it is easy to imagine four separate compartments behind the four faces. The cube is one hollow container of water, which puts every face at the same temperature. That is the whole design of the apparatus: it removes temperature as a variable so that the nature of the surface is the only thing left to explain the difference.
items.random_wrong: The shiny silver face, because polished metal gives out infrared best.

items.q: A student compares the infrared radiation emitted by the four faces of a Leslie cube. Which change would most improve the investigation?
items.correct: Keep the detector the same distance from every face when reading it.
items.misconception: Move the detector closer to the darker faces so their readings are clearer.
items.why: Students see the detector as reading a property of the surface rather than as measuring the radiation arriving at one particular place, so its position looks like a matter of convenience. The detector measures the infrared arriving where it stands, which depends on distance as well as on the surface. Fix the distance with a ruler and keep it for all four faces, so that the surface is the only variable being changed.
items.random_wrong: Take the reading from each of the faces at a different water temperature.

items.q: Four identical cans are painted matt black, matt white, shiny silver and dull grey. Each is filled with cold water and placed the same distance from a radiant heater. Which can's water warms fastest?
items.correct: The matt black can, because it is the best absorber of infrared.
items.misconception: The shiny silver can, because a polished metal surface takes radiation in best.
items.why: Students merge radiation with conduction. A metal does feel cold and does conduct well, and that experience is transferred to a question about radiation, where the polished surface in fact reflects. Conduction and radiation are different transfers. What matters for infrared arriving at a surface is whether the surface absorbs or reflects it: matt black absorbs almost all of it, polished silver reflects almost all of it.
items.random_wrong: All four cans equally, because the heater is the same distance away.

items.q: A ray of light travels through air and strikes the flat surface of a glass block at an angle to the normal. Light travels more slowly in glass than in air. Which statement correctly describes the refracted ray inside the glass?
items.correct: It bends towards the normal, because it slows down in the glass.
items.misconception: It bends away from the normal as it enters the glass.
items.why: The two boundaries of a rectangular block look alike on a diagram, so the pair of bends is memorised as a shape without the rule that fixes which way round they go. Students then draw the pair in reverse. Tie the direction of bending to the change of speed: slowing down bends the ray towards the normal, speeding up bends it away. Air into glass is slowing down, so the ray bends towards the normal.
items.random_wrong: It carries straight on undeviated, changing only its speed.

items.q: A wave slows down as it enters a new medium. Do the wave fronts get closer together or further apart?
items.correct: Closer together. The frequency is unchanged and the speed has fallen, so the wavelength — which is the spacing of the fronts — falls too.
items.misconception: A slower wave has fronts that are further apart, because slowing something down spreads it out.
items.why: Students borrow an image from traffic or from a queue, where things that slow down are imagined to spread out. They also confuse the spacing of the fronts with the time between them, which is unchanged. The fronts leave the boundary at the same rate as they arrive, because the frequency is fixed. Each front then travels a shorter distance before the next one is produced, so the spacing shrinks in the slower medium.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A matt black surface is the best absorber of infrared. Is it a good emitter too?
items.correct: Yes. A good absorber of infrared radiation is also a good emitter of it, so the matt black face of a Leslie cube gives the largest detector reading.
items.misconception: Black surfaces soak radiation up and hold on to it, so they are good absorbers but poor emitters; shiny or pale surfaces are thought to give radiation out best.
items.why: Absorption is met first, in the context of black clothing feeling hot in the sun, and 'soaking up' suggests keeping. Emission is then treated as a separate, unrelated property of the surface. Absorption and emission go together: whatever a surface is good at taking in, it is equally good at giving out. Matt black is the best at both and shiny silver is the worst at both.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all electromagnetic waves travel at the same velocity in every substance?
items.correct: No. They all travel at the same velocity through a vacuum, but the velocity in a substance depends on the substance, and on the wavelength as well.
items.misconception: Electromagnetic waves always travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s, so their velocity can never differ from one substance to another.
items.why: The single value quoted for the speed of electromagnetic waves is learned without the phrase 'in a vacuum' attached to it, and it is repeated so often that it hardens into a universal constant of the wave itself. The common value applies in a vacuum, and very nearly in air. In glass or water the velocity is lower, and it is exactly that difference in velocity between two substances that causes refraction at the boundary.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the angle of refraction the angle between the incident ray and the refracted ray?
items.correct: No. The angle of refraction is measured between the refracted ray and the normal, on the far side of the boundary.
items.misconception: The angle of refraction means the amount by which the ray has been bent, so it is the angle between the ray's old direction and its new one.
items.why: The everyday sense of 'refraction' is the bending itself, so 'angle of refraction' is read as 'angle of bend'. On a diagram both rays are already drawn in, which makes that the easy angle to measure. Both named angles are measured from the normal: the angle of incidence between the incident ray and the normal, the angle of refraction between the refracted ray and the normal. The angle of bend is the difference between them and has no name in the specification.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A ray enters a glass block at an angle to the normal. Does it just slow down and carry straight on?
items.correct: No. Because it meets the boundary at an angle it also changes direction, bending towards the normal as it slows.
items.misconception: Entering glass only changes the wave's speed, so a slanted ray simply slows down and continues in a straight line.
items.why: Students learn that refraction is caused by a change of speed and conclude that speed is the only thing that changes, so the change of direction that gives refraction its name is dropped. A change of speed at an angled boundary produces a change of direction: one end of the wave front is slowed before the other, so a slanted ray bends towards the normal rather than continuing straight.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a ray of light meets the surface of a glass block at an angle, does it bounce off instead of going in?
items.correct: No. Glass transmits visible light, so most of the ray crosses into the block and is refracted; it does not simply reflect off the surface.
items.misconception: A ray meeting a glass surface reflects off it, like light from a mirror, rather than passing into the glass and refracting.
items.why: Reflection at a shiny surface is met before refraction, and a glass block looks reflective, so students expect the ray to bounce rather than enter and bend. A transparent block transmits most of the light reaching it, and that light crosses the boundary and refracts. Some reflection does occur, but only for a small part of the ray, which is not what a refraction ray diagram shows.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
